rationale: B wins because it found the real pressure point in the launch: "The installer bottleneck: a home battery that claims it skips the rewiring," then built reporter shape around contractors, permitting, install hours, and jurisdictions. A is strong, but "A profitable public electronics giant is funding its own move into home energy" smuggles in a financing claim the update does not give and is less reportable than the installer and homeowner math B surfaced. Both avoid the usual revolutionary-ecosystem sludge; B just gives the founder more usable doors into a newsroom.
gaps_in_A: "self-funding entry" is not in the update; profitable and publicly traded does not prove how Anker is financing the move.

"That is a concrete competitive claim a reporter can pressure-test against Powerwall's install profile" cages the strongest differentiator inside a Tesla comparison; the cleaner beat is installers, permitting, labor, and install cost.

No real buyer/payback angle despite the supplied facts that the system can "run a home during outages" and "cut peak-rate bills"; A refuses fake savings but never builds the honest consumer-finance version.
"any second consumer-electronics maker making the same move" admits the category claim is one-company-thin unless outside proof appears.
gaps_in_B: "Soft costs and electrician scarcity are the recurring problem in that beat" is outside the supplied facts; source it or phrase it as a reporting question.
"changes the price floor of home storage" is a good hypothesis, but without price per usable kWh it is a trap dressed as a story.
"What a homeowner is actually buying when they buy backup power" is useful, but not pitchable as a customer-story until there is "one real US household" with real bill and install-cost data.
